mn10:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the Kuru country. There is town of theirs called Kammāssadamma,
mn10:1.3: and there he addressed the bhikkhus thus:
mn10:2.1: ‘Bhikkhus, this path, namely the four foundations of mindfulness, is a path that goes in one way only: to the purification of beings, to the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, to the disappearance of pain and grief, to the attainment of the true way, to the realization of Nibbāna.
mn10:3.2: Here a bhikkhu abides contemplating a body as a body fully aware and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.
mn10:3.3: He abides contemplating feelings as feelings, ardent, fully aware and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.
mn10:3.4: He abides contemplating mind as mind, ardent, fully aware and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.
mn10:3.5: He abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas, ardent, fully aware and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.
mn10:4.1: ‘And how does a bhikkhu abide contemplationg the body as a body?
mn10:4.2: ‘Here a bhikkhu, gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, established mindfulness (on the breath) in front of him,
mn10:4.3: always mindful he breaths in, mindful he breathes out.
mn10:4.4: ‘Breathing in long, he understands: “I breathe in long”; breathing out long, he understands: “I breathe out long”.
mn10:4.5: Breathing in short, he understands: “I breathe in short”; breathing out short, he understands: “I breathe out short”.
mn10:4.6: He trains thus: “I shall breathe in experiencing a whole body”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out experiencing a whole body”.
mn10:4.7: He trains thus: “I shall breathe in tranquillizing the body process”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out tranquillizing the bodily process”.
mn10:4.8: ‘Just as skilled turner or his apprentice, when making a long turn understands: “I make a long turn”; or when making a short turn understands: “I make a short turn”;
mn10:4.9: so too, breathing in long, he understands: “I breathe in long”: …
mn10:4.11: he trains thus: “I shall breathe out tranquillizing the bodily process”.
mn10:5.1: ‘In this way he abides contemplating the body as a body in himself, or he abides contemplating the body as a body externally, or he abides contemplating the body in himself and externally.
mn10:5.2: ‘Or else he abides contemplating in the body its arising factors, or he abides contemplating in the body its vanishing factors, or he abides contemplating in the body its arising and vanishing factors.
mn10:5.3: ‘Or else mindfulness that “there is a body” is simply established in him to the extent of bare knowledge and remembrance (of it), while he abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world.
mn10:5.4: ‘That is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating the body as a body.
mn10:6.1: ‘Again, a bhikkhu, when walking, understands: “I walk”; when standing, understands: “I stand”; when sitting, understands: “I sit”; when lying down, understands: “I am lying down”;
mn10:6.2: or however his body is disposed he understands accordingly.
mn10:7.1: ‘… contemplating … in himself … externally … in himself and externally.
mn10:7.2: ‘… contemplating … arising factors … vanishing factors … arising and vanishing factors.
mn10:7.3: ‘… mindfulness that “there is a body” … not clinging to anything in the world.
mn10:7.4: ‘That also is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating the body as a body.
mn10:8.1: ‘Again, a bhikkhu is one who acts in full awareness when moving to and fro, who acts in full awareness when looking at and away, who acts in full awareness when flexing and extending, who acts in full awareness when wearing the patched cloak, bowl and robes, who acts in full awareness when feeding, drinking, chewing and supping, who acts in full awareness when evacuating the bowels and making water, who acts in full awareness when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, talking, and keeping silent.
mn10:9.1: ‘… contemplating … in himself … externally … in himself and externally … contemplating … arising factors … vanishing factors … arising and vanishing factors … mindfulness that ‘there is a body’ … not clinging to anything in the world.
mn10:9.2: ‘That also is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating the body as a body.
mn10:10.1: ‘Again, a bhikkhu reviews this same body up from the soles of the feet and down from the top of the hair as full of many kinds of filth, thus:
mn10:10.2: “In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs, bowels, entrails, gorge, dung, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints and urine.”’
mn10:10.3: ‘Just as though there were a bag with an opening at both (ends) full of many sorts of grain such as hill rice, red rice, beans, peas, millet and white rice, and a man with (clear) eyes had opened it and were reviewing it thus: “This is hill rice, this is red rice, these are beans, these are peas, this is millet, this is white rice”,
mn10:10.4: so too, a bhikkhu reviews this same body up from the soles of the feet and down from the top of the hair as full of many kinds of filth …
mn10:11.1: ‘ … contemplating … in himself … externally … in himself and externally … contemplatng … arising factors … vanishing factors … arising and vanishing factors … mindfulness that “there is a body” … not clinging to anything in the world.
mn10:12.1: ‘Again, however it is placed, however disposed, a bhikkhu reviews this same body (consisting of) elements, thus:
mn10:12.2: “In this body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.”
mn10:12.3: ‘Just as though a skilled butcher or his apprentice had a killed a cow and were seated at the four crossroads with it cut up into pieces:
mn10:12.4: so too, however it is placed, however disposed, a bhikkhu reviews this same body … and the air element.
mn10:12.5: “In this body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.”
mn10:13.1: ‘ … contemplating … in himself … externally … in himself and externally … contemplating … arising factors … arising and vanishing factors … mindfulness that “there is a body” … not clinging to anything in the world.
mn10:14.1: ‘Again, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground, one day dead, two days dead, three days dead, bloated, livid, and oozing matter,
mn10:14.3: “This body too is of such a nature, it will be like that, it is not exempt from that.”
mn10:15.1: ‘ … contemplating … in himself … not clinging to anything in the world.
mn10:16.1: ‘Again, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground, being devoured by crows, kites, vultures, dogs, jackals, and the multitudinous kinds of worms,
mn10:16.3: “This body too is of such a nature, it will be like that, it is not exempt from that.”
mn10:17.1: ‘... contemplating ... in himself ... not clinging to anything in the world.’
mn10:18.1: ‘Again, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground, a skeleton with flesh and blood held together with sinews, thus: “This body too is of such a nature...”’
mn10:19.1: ‘Again, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground, a fleshless skeleton smeared with blood and held together with sinews, ...’
mn10:20.1: ‘Again, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground, a skeleton without flesh and blood held together with sinews ...’
mn10:24.1: ‘Again, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground, bones without sinews scattered in all directions, here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone, there a thigh-bone, there a hip-bone, there a back-bone, there a rib-bone, there a breast-bone, there an arm-bone, there a shoulder-bone, there a neck-bone, there a jaw-bone, there a tooth-bone, there the skull ...’
mn10:25.1: ‘... contemplating ... in himself ... not clinging to anything in the world.’
mn10:26-28.1: ‘Again, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground, bones bleached white, the colour of shells ...’
mn10:29.1: ‘Again, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown in a charnel ground, bones heaped up, more than a year old ...
mn10:30.1: ‘Again, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown in a charnel ground, bones rotted and crumbled to dust,
mn10:30.3: “This body too is of such a nature, it will be like that, it is not exempt from that.”
mn10:31.1: ‘In this way he abides contemplating the body as a body in himself, or he abides contemplating the body as a body externally, or he abides contemplating the body as a body in himself and externally.
mn10:31.2: ‘Or else he abides contemplating in the body its arising factors, or he abides contemplating in the body its vanishing factors, or he abides contemplating in the body its arising and vanishing factors.
mn10:31.3: ‘Or else mindfulness that “there is a body” is simply established in him to the extent of bare knowledge and remembrance (of it), while he abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world.
mn10:31.4: ‘That also is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating the body as a body.
mn10:32.1: ‘And how does a bhikkhu abide contemplating feelings as feelings?
mn10:32.2: ‘Here, when feeling a pleasant feeling, a bhikkhu undertsands: “I feel a pleasant feeling”;
mn10:32.3: when feeling a painful feeling, he understands: “I feel a painful feeling”;
mn10:32.4: when feeling a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: “I feel a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling”.
mn10:32.5: When feeling a materialistic pleasant feeling he understands: “I feel a materialistic pleasant feeling”;
mn10:32.6: when feeling an unmaterialistic pleasant feeling,, he understands: “I feel an unmaterialistic pleasant feeling”;
mn10:32.7: when feeling a materialistic painful feeling, he understands: “I feel a materialistic painful feeling;
mn10:32.8: when feeling an unmaterialistic painful feeling, he understands: “I feel an unmaterialistic painful feeling”;
mn10:32.9: when feeling a materialistic neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: “I feel a materialistic neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling”;
mn10:32.10: when feeling an unmaterialistic neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: “I feel an unmaterialistic neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling”.
mn10:33.1: ‘In this way he abides contemplating feelings as feelings in himself, or he abides contemplating feelings as feelings externally, or he abides contemplating feelings as feelings in himself and externally.
mn10:33.2: ‘Or else he abides contemplating in feeling its arising factors, or he abides contemplating in feeling its vanishing factors, or he abides contemplating in feeling its arising and vanishing factors.
mn10:33.3: ‘Or else mindfulness that “there is feeling” is simply established in him to the extent of bare knowledge and remembrance (of it), while he abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world.
mn10:33.4: ‘That is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating feelings as feelings.
mn10:34.1: ‘And how does a bhikkhu abide contemplating mind as mind?
mn10:34.2: ‘Here a bhikkhu understands mind affected by lust as affected by lust,
mn10:34.3: and mind unaffected by lust as unaffected by lust.
mn10:34.4: He under-stands mind affected by hate as affected by hate,
mn10:34.5: and mind unaffected by hate as unaffected by hate.
mn10:34.6: He understands mind affected by delusion as affected by delusion,
mn10:34.7: and mind unaffected by delusion as unaffected by delusion.
mn10:34.8: He understands contracted mind as contracted,
mn10:34.10: He understands exalted mind as exalted,
mn10:34.12: He understands surpassed mind as surpassed,
mn10:34.14: He understands concentrated mind as concentrated,
mn10:34.16: He understands liberated mind as liberated
mn10:35.1: ‘In this way he abides contemplating mind as mind in himself, or he abides contemplating mind as mind externally, or he abides contemplating mind as mind in himself and externally.
mn10:35.2: ‘Or else he abides contemplating in the mind its arising factors, or he abides contemplating in the mind its vanishing factors, or he abides contemplating in the mind its arising and vanishing factors.
mn10:35.3: ‘Or else mindfulness that “there is a mind” is simply established in him to the extent of bare knowledge and remembrance (of it), while he abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world.
mn10:35.4: ‘That is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating the mind as mind.
mn10:36.1: ‘And how does a bhikkhu abide contemplating dhammas as dhammas?
mn10:36.2: ‘Here a bhikkhu abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the five hindrances.
mn10:36.3: ‘How does a bhikkhu abide contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the five hindrances?
mn10:36.4: ‘Here, there being desire for sensual pleasures in him, a bhikkhu understands: “There is desire for sensual pleasures in me”, or there being no desire for sensual pleasures in him, he understands: “There is no desire for sensual pleasures in me”, and also he understands how there comes to be the arising of unarisen desire for sensual pleasures, and he understands how there comes to be the abandoning of arisen desire for sensual pleasures, and he understands how there comes to be the future non-arising of abandoned desire for sensual pleasures.
mn10:36.8: ‘There being uncertainty in him … the future non-arising of abandoned uncertainty.
mn10:37.1: ‘In this way he abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in himself, or he abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas externally, or he abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in himself and externally.
mn10:37.2: ‘Or else he abides contemplating in dhammas their arising factors, or he abides contemplating in dhammas their vanishing factors, or he abides contemplating in dhammas their arising and vanishing factors
mn10:37.3: ‘Or else mindfulness that “there are dhammas” is simply established in him to the extent of bare knowledge and remembrance (of it), while he abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world.
mn10:37.4: ‘That is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the five hindrances.
mn10:38.1: ‘Again, a bhikkhu abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the five aggregates affected by clinging.
mn10:38.2: ‘And how does a bhikkhu abide contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the five aggregates affected by clinging?
mn10:38.4: “Such is form, such its origin, such its disappearance;
mn10:38.5: such is feeling, such its origin, such its disappearance;
mn10:38.6: such is perception, such its origin, such its disappearance;
mn10:38.7: such is formations, such their origin, such their disappearance;
mn10:38.8: such is consciousness, such its origin, such its disappearance”.
mn10:39.1: ‘… contemplating … in himself … externally … in himself and externally …
mn10:39.2: contemplating … arising factors … vanishing factors … arising and vanishing factors …
mn10:39.3: mindfulness that “there are dhammas” … not clinging to anything in the world.
mn10:40.1: ‘Again, a bhikkhu abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the six in-oneself/external bases.
mn10:40.2: ‘And how does a bhikkhu abide contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the six in-oneself/external bases?
mn10:40.3: ‘Here a bhikkhu understands the eye, he understands forms, and he understands the fetter that arises dependent on both; he understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen fetter, he understands how there comes to be the abandoning of the arisen fetter, and he understands how there comes to be the future non-arising of the abandoned fetter.
mn10:40.4: ‘He understands the ear, he understands sounds …
mn10:40.5: ‘He understands the nose, he understands odours …
mn10:40.6: ‘He understands the tongue, he understands flavours …
mn10:40.7: ‘He understands the body, he understands tangibles …
mn10:40.8: ‘He understands the mind, he understands dhammas, and he understands the fetter that arises dependent on both, he understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen fetter, he understands how there comes to be the abandoning of the arisen fetter, and he understands how there comes to be the future non-arising of the abandoned fetter.
mn10:41.1: ‘… contemplating … in himself … externally … in himself and externally …
mn10:41.2: contemplating … arising factors … vanishing factors … arising and vanishing factors …
mn10:41.3: mindfulness that “there are dhammas” … not clinging to anything in the world.
mn10:42.1: ‘Again, a bhikkhu abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the seven enlightenment factors.
mn10:42.2: ‘And how he does a bhikkhu abide contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the seven enlightenment factors?
mn10:42.3: ‘Here, there being the mindfulness enlightenment factor in him, a bhikkhu understands: “There is the mindfulness enlightenment factor in me”, there being no mindfulness enlightenment factor in him, he understands: “There is no mindfulness enlightenment factor in me”; and also he understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen mindfulness enlightenment factor, and he understands how the arisen mindfulness enlightenment factor comes to be developed and perfected.
mn10:42.4: ‘There being the investigation-of-dhammas enlightenment factor in him …
mn10:42.5: ‘There being the energy enlightenment factor in him …
mn10:42.6: ‘There being the happiness factor in him …
mn10:42.7: ‘There being the tranquillity enlightenment factor in him …
mn10:42.8: ‘There being the concentration enlightenment factor in him …
mn10:42.9: ‘There being the equanimity enlightenment factor in him … he understands: “There is the equanimity enlightenment factor in me”, there being no equanimity enlightenment factor in him, he understands: “There is no equanimity enlightenment factor in me”, and also he understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen equanimity enlightenment factor, and he understands how the arisen equanimity enlightenment factor comes to be developed and perfected.
mn10:43.1: ‘… contemplating … in himself … externally … in himself and externally …
mn10:43.2: contemplating … arising factors … vanishing factors … arising and vanishing factors …
mn10:43.3: mindfulness that “there are dhammas” … not clinging to anything in the world.
mn10:44.1: ‘Again, a bhikkhu abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the Four Noble Truths.
mn10:44.2: ‘And how does a bhikkhu abide contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the Four Noble Truths?
mn10:44.3: ‘Here a bhikkhu understands as it actually is that: “Such is suffering”; he understands as it actually is: “Such is the origin of suffering”; he understands as it actually is: “Such is the cessation of suffering”; he understands as it actually is: “Such is the way leading to the cessation of suffering”.
mn10:45.1: ‘In this way he abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in himself, or he abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas externally, or he abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in himself and externally.
mn10:45.2: ‘Or else he abides contemplating in dhammas their arising factors, or he abides contemplating in dhammas their vanishing factors or he abides contemplating in dhammas their arising and vanishing factors.
mn10:45.3: ‘Or else mindfulness that “there are dhammas” is simply established in him to the extent of bare knowledge and remembrance (of it), while he abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world.
mn10:45.4: ‘That is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas in (terms of) the Four Noble Truths.
mn10:46.1: ‘Bhikkhus, were anyone to develop these four foundations of mindfulness for seven years, one of two fruits could be expected for him:
mn10:46.2: either final knowledge here and now, or if there is a trace of clinging left, non-return.
mn10:46.4: were anyone to develop these four foundations for six years …
mn10:46.5: ‘Let alone six years … for five years …
mn10:46.6: ‘Let alone five years … for four years …
mn10:46.7: ‘Let alone four years … for three years …
mn10:46.8: ‘Let alone three years … for two years …
mn10:46.9: ‘Let alone two years … for one year …
mn10:46.15: ‘Let alone six months … for five months …
mn10:46.16: ‘Let alone five months … for four months …
mn10:46.17: ‘Let alone four months … for three months …
mn10:46.18: ‘Let alone three months … for two months …
mn10:46.19: ‘Let alone two months … for one month …
mn10:46.20: ‘Let alone one month … for half a month …
mn10:46.22: were anyone to develop these four foundations of mindfulness for seven days, one of two fruits could be expected for him:
mn10:46.23: either final knowledge here and now, or if there is a trace of clinging left, non-return.
mn10:47.1: “Bhikkhus, this path, namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, is a path that he goes in one way only: to the purification of beings, to the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, to the disappearance of pain and grief, to the attainment of the true way, to the realization of Nibbāna.”’
mn10:47.2: So it was in reference to this that it was said:
mn10:47.3: That is what the Blessed One said.
mn10:47.4: The bhikkhus were satisfied, and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
